Abstract

Debates over return-to-office mandates have intensified since the COVID-19 pandemic ended, though their economic implications remain poorly understood. Using large-scale resume data, we analyze how these policies affect employee tenure and seniority at three large U.S. tech companies: Microsoft, SpaceX, and Apple. Employing a distributional synthetic controls framework, we estimate a reduction in tenure and seniority at firms returning to the office. We extend the framework with a functional bootstrap procedure and prove its validity for constructing uniform confidence bands. Return-to-office mandates appear to drive senior employees away, posing a risk to firm productivity and innovation.

JEL Codes: J21, J62, M54, C14

Keywords: causal inference, distributional synthetic controls, human capital, return to office, seniority, tenure, work from home

sections.name: Introduction
sections.text:
Since the World Health Organization officially declared an end to the COVID-19 health crisis, companies have shifted their focus towards creating workplace policies for a post-pandemic economy. In this, the preferences of employers and employees often seem diametrically opposed. That opposition has expressed itself most notably in the debate around the effects of the return to office (RTO). This debate is far from settled: as of June 2023, an estimated 75% of tech and 28% of all companies in the United States were still “fully flexible” – either fully remote or with a voluntary in-office option (Scoop, 2023). Most business executives expect this number to grow (Bloom, Barrero, Davis, Meyer and Mihaylov, 2023a). In this paper, we provide causal evidence that RTO mandates at three large tech companies—Microsoft, SpaceX, and Apple—had a negative effect on the tenure and seniority of their respective workforces. In particular, we find the strongest negative effects at the top of the distribution, implying a more pronounced exodus of relatively senior personnel.

To do so, we estimate the composition of the workforce in the counterfactual reality where the company did not implement an RTO mandate. We document changes in the employee composition that can profoundly impact a company, especially since these changes occur at the top of the hierarchy. Senior employees and those that have been at a company for a long time possess invaluable human capital and tend to have elevated productivity levels (Lazear et al., 2015), which they take with them when leaving the company. They also represent a significant investment in terms of hiring and training costs (Blatter et al., 2012). Indeed, the central tenet of resource-based theory, one of the most prevalent and empirically well-supported human capital theories, is that human capital is key to explaining why some firms outperform others (Crook et al., 2011). Changes in the employee distributions can, moreover, have ripple effects in the larger economy, by affecting the distribution of skilled workers across different types of companies (Lise and Robin, 2017; Eeckhout and Kircher, 2018).

We uncover these results by estimating the distributional causal effects of a return-to-office mandate on the makeup of a company’s workforce using a synthetic controls approach (Abadie and Gardeazabal, 2003; Abadie et al., 2010). Since our object of interest is the heterogeneity in the composition of the workforce of a company, we employ the distributional synthetic controls estimator proposed in Gunsilius (2023). Our ability to account for the heterogeneity in the organizational structure of companies is of fundamental importance in this setting. This estimator is also ideally suited for this setting, since it does not require observing the same individuals over time and as such allows for the very changes in workforce composition that we are interested in. Furthermore, it provides a nonparametric estimate of the effect of an RTO on the entire tenure and seniority distribution of a target company. Beyond applying this estimator, we make three methodological contributions. First, we develop bootstrap-based uniform confidence bands and prove their validity under regularity conditions (Appendix E), allowing researchers to identify which parts of a distribution show statistically significant effects; mathematically, this contribution is completely novel in that it provides bootstrapped confidence intervals for these types of functional data, namely replicated quantile function processes. Second, we extend the methodology to ordinal categorical outcomes (like job titles) by working with mixtures of distributions rather than mixtures of quantiles. Third, we propose a ratio-based permutation test that accounts for differential pre-treatment fit quality across placebo units.

Our case-study approach focuses on Microsoft, Apple, and SpaceX because they were among the first large American tech companies to implement RTO mandates. In particular, they did so before a wave of layoffs started hitting the tech industry from late 2022 onwards, allowing us to cleanly disentangle the causal effects of the RTO mandates. Our synthetic controls approach, moreover, allows us to study in detail what happens within each company after an RTO, which would not be possible with an aggregate cross-company approach. This guarantees the internal validity of our estimates. Their external validity is twofold. First, we consider some of the largest companies in a sector where the discourse over the return to office was most heated. Together, the three companies account for over 2% of employment in the tech sector and 30% of its revenue. What happens at these companies matters for the American economy, and sets the precedent for the wider debate around the return to office. Second, we estimate very similar effects for all three companies despite their markedly different corporate culture and product gamut, suggesting the effects are driven by common underlying dynamics. Nonetheless, an important limitation of this case-study design is that the estimates are most directly informative about early RTO mandates at these three large U.S. technology firms under the relatively tight labor-market conditions of 2022. We therefore interpret the results as internally valid evidence for these settings rather than as an unconditional average effect of RTO mandates across all firms, industries, or labor-market regimes.

Our paper contributes to several branches of the literature. First, it addresses the relatively understudied impact of RTO mandates. For instance, Ding and Ma (2023) analyze the determinants and effects of RTO mandates for a sample of S&P 500 companies by examining company balance sheets and Glassdoor reviews. They suggest that RTOs are used by managers to reassert control, which in turn reduces employee satisfaction. Using a voluntary survey of managers and their employees, van Triest (2023) demonstrates that work-from-home (WFH) levels are 50% lower when managers have the discretion to set RTO policies, as opposed to being constrained by organization-wide rules. Barrero et al. (2021) report that four out of ten employees working from home would find a new job under an RTO mandate, based on a large-scale survey of American workers. Several business and industry reports have also studied RTO. For example, a large-scale survey by Unispace (2023) found that almost half of firms with mandated RTOs experienced higher than usual difficulties in retaining employees and lost “key” staff members, in line with our findings. In another survey of over 3,500 employees, one in three executives said they would leave their job if faced with an RTO mandate, compared to 19% of non-executives (Gartner, 2024). Our paper complements and extends this literature by estimating a significant outflow of more senior employees after the implementation of an RTO mandate. Unlike these previous studies, we rely on large-scale resume data rather than surveys, allowing us to study the realized consequences of RTO policies rather than self-reported behavior, intentions, or preferences. Moreover, the richness of our data and estimation approach allows us to speak to causal rather than merely descriptive effects. It also allows us to study what happens to the organizational structure of companies that return to the office, which is a first-order effect of such a return.

Second, our paper relates to the large literature on WFH. Focusing on the impact of WFH on employee tenure and seniority, this body of work provides several insights relevant to ours.11
1

For a comprehensive survey of the effects of WFH, we refer to Ding and Ma (2023, §2.3) and Barrero et al. (2023). Mas and Pallais (2017) estimate, using an experimental design, that workers had a willingness to pay for hybrid work arrangements of around 8% of total pay before the pandemic, with a fat tail of high-valuation workers. Emanuel et al. (2023) find that proximity to coworkers in the office increases the feedback software engineers receive but reduces their programming output, especially for senior engineers. Hansen et al. (2023) study hybrid work options in large-scale job postings data and find substantial heterogeneity within occupation and even company. Mischke et al. (2023) and Barrero et al. (2023) find that office attendance is lower in larger firms, in line with our finding that employees leave for such firms at higher rates after an RTO. Barrero et al. (2022) find that a shift to remote work puts downward pressure on wages due to lower employee turnover, which may have reduced the college wage premium as highly educated workers are more likely to WFH (Barrero et al., 2023). Finally, Bloom, Han and Liang (2023) document lower attrition rates under a hybrid work model compared to a fully-in-person one.

An important distinction between our focus on RTO mandates and the WFH literature is that we consider the effects of a mandatory shift to (partial) office attendance from an optional hybrid model, while the WFH literature has mostly focused on static comparisons between fully-remote, hybrid, and fully-in-person work. Moreover, while several of the papers mentioned have documented a positive relation between employee attrition rates and degree of required office attendance, our results illuminate how this attrition realizes across the employee distribution, with senior and long-tenured employees leaving at higher rates. Considering the pivotal role such employees play in a company’s development and competitive edge, along with the significant costs involved in replacing the firm-specific human capital accumulated over their tenure (Gerhart and Feng, 2021), our findings indicate that such “uneven” attrition should be a major concern for any company considering a return to office.

The rest of this paper is structured as follows. In Section 2 we discuss our empirical approach in terms of data and estimation and present some descriptive evidence; in Section 3 we present our causal results and discuss their implications in light of the academic literature; before concluding in Section 4.

sections.name: People Data Labs
sections.text:
We study the impact of RTO across the employee distribution using data provided by People Data Labs (PDL) (https://www.peopledatalabs.com/) via the Dewey Data platform (https://deweydata.io/) (People Data Labs, 2022). The dataset consists of global resume data for nearly 1 billion unique individuals, with 1.2 billion person records in North America from over 300 million resumes. At the companies of interest, Microsoft, Apple, and SpaceX, we observe 49,083, 29,297, and 2,807 resumes in the quarter immediately preceding each RTO, respectively. The data contain information on the start and end date of a person’s position at a given company, as well as the role (trainee, entry, partner, etc.) of the position.

The data are obtained from a wide variety of sources, comprising two main categories:22
2

See https://docs.peopledatalabs.com/docs/data-sources for more details. first, publicly available data, which includes career websites such as LinkedIn (over 700 million profiles globally), social media platforms such as Facebook (over 1 billion profiles) and Twitter (over 50 million profiles), as well as public records and publicly available government data; second, PDL’s ‘‘Data Union’’, which is a proprietary data-sharing co-op through which some of PDL’s clients share their internal data in a confidential and secure manner. These clients include companies in HR and Real Estate tech as well as in the identity and anti-fraud industries. Because records are often obtained directly from employer systems in these industries, they may be more complete than self-reported online profiles, though we cannot verify this directly. Moreover, many of the clients in the Data Union are software companies, which means that, in practice, we observe a substantial share of employees for most companies in our sample of tech firms. PDL cross-references all these sources, deduplicates them, and assesses their quality through a battery of tests.33
3

See https://docs.peopledatalabs.com/docs/data-accuracy for more information. To assess coverage, we manually collected data on the reported US headcount in 2022 at the 32 firms in our main estimation sample. We collected these data from public company statements and SEC filings, using information from company statements about US-specific growth to estimate the US-specific headcount when only global headcount figures were available. Comparing these headcounts to the corresponding resume counts in the PDL data, we find that our dataset covers 52% of a firm’s employment in our sample, on average, with a median of 57% and a minimum of 8%. For Microsoft, Apple, and SpaceX specifically, we observe resumes of 42%, 29%, and 24% of their estimated US workforce in 2022, respectively (see Table A-15). Importantly, our identification strategy does not require the PDL sample to be perfectly representative. For the estimated effect to recover the corresponding effect for the underlying workforce population, the distortion induced by selection into the PDL data must be replicated by the synthetic control. Thus, even systematic over- or under-sampling of certain worker types need not bias the population contrast when the resulting selection distortion is balanced between the treated firm and its synthetic control. We characterize this requirement formally through an exact decomposition of selection bias in Appendix F.

We further sum this variable across multiple subsequent employment episodes at the same company for the same individual, to calculate total tenure for a single employment spell. This is needed because employees tend to list a single employment spell at the same company under separate resume items to indicate promotions.

As another proxy for seniority within the company, we use the discrete distribution of job titles in the PDL data. The lowest level is “unpaid” and the highest “CXO”, corresponding to a C-suite title. The full list of titles and their corresponding numeric codes is shown in Table 1. We define an employee’s title within a given quarter as the highest title they held within the company in that quarter.

sections.name: Return to Office
sections.text:
We collect data on the return to office dates of tech firms from two sources. First, we manually collect information on the month a return-to-office mandate was implemented for 55 large tech firms (e.g. Google, Apple, IBM) based on news reports and leaks on a popular anonymous employee forum, Blind. Firms were selected based on market capitalization and availability of public information on their RTO policies. Of the firms considered, 19 implemented an RTO mandate, while the other 36 continued to allow remote work to varying degrees as of February 2023. Here, “RTO mandate” denotes any degree of mandated office attendance, from 1 day a week to full-time. We depict the chronology of the return to office dates we collected in Figure 1. Though this is not necessarily a representative sample, we can see that RTO implementations only picked up more rapidly from spring 2023 onwards.

Second, we supplement this list with data scraped from the Flex Index by Scoop Technologies, a hybrid working platform (https://www.flex.scoopforwork.com/). At the time we scraped them (Feb 2024), these data provided information on the remote work arrangements of more than 8,000 companies. While they do not contain information on the date these companies returned to work (if at all), we leverage these data to expand our set of “never-treated” companies that never returned to the office. These serve as our control units, together with companies that were “not-yet-treated” until 3 months after the end of our sample period. We were able to match these data directly to the PDL data based on the company name and website domain, as both fields had accurate coverage in the two datasets. In Table A-1, we list all the control firms used in our main estimation sample for Microsoft, and their corresponding RTO policies at the time of writing. The table also provides verification of these policies against two independent sources, to make sure the Scoop data is accurate: 1) the RTO dates collected by Flynn et al. (2024) from Factiva for the Russell 3000;44
4

We thank the authors for sharing their data with us. 2) publicly available news reports, for which we provide links. That way, we provide independent verification of the Scoop data from at least one source for every control firm in our main sample.

sections.name: Tech Layoffs
sections.text: The tech sector in the United States has experienced persistent rounds of large-scale layoffs since late 2022 that continued well into 2024. As these layoffs were in general independent of companies’ RTO mandates, they are likely to confound our estimates. Of course, an employee’s refusal to comply with an RTO mandate could affect their likelihood of being laid off, but this does not affect the independence of the implementation of both policies. To address this concern, we leverage data from layoffs.fyi, a website that has tracked the near-universe of tech sector layoffs since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. The website aggregates information on layoffs from news reports, company announcements, and crowdsourced employee reports. We match these data to the PDL data with a combination of fuzzy string matching and manual checking to ascertain we capture all layoffs in the data.

sections.name: Sample Construction
sections.text:
We begin by identifying the relevant set of “treated units” used in the main estimation. To avoid concurrent shocks during the estimation window, we restrict the set of firms to companies without layoffs during the two quarters before and one quarter after their RTO mandate. This restriction yields three firms: Microsoft, SpaceX, and Apple. We emphasize that the synthetic control method used in this paper, introduced below, is fundamentally a case-study approach, which emphasizes internal over external validity. As such, it is natural to focus on a small number of influential firms for which we can validly identify causal effects (see the discussion in the introduction).
To that extent, note that all three companies implemented their RTO mandate relatively early, before both layoffs and the larger return to office debate heated up in the American tech sector. They all implemented several rounds of layoffs as well, but, as mentioned, only did so at least one quarter after their return to office. Moreover, they are all large tech firms that produce both hardware and software and employ several thousands of people. All three companies also shifted from an optional hybrid model to mandatory office attendance. The degree of office presence mandated varied, with Microsoft mandating 50% attendance (O’Loughlin, 2022; Tilley and Cutter, 2022; Rosenblatt, 2022; Cohen, 2024), Apple requiring 1 day a week (O’Loughlin, 2023; Lyons, 2022), and SpaceX demanding full-time attendance (40 hours per week) (Mac, 2022). We replicate our main results for these three companies, but focus on Microsoft throughout the paper as it has the largest numbers of resumes in our data, it was the first to implement an RTO among the three companies, and its RTO was the “cleanest” and most clearly announced – with Apple postponing its increase from 1 to 3 days a week until September 2022 (O’Loughlin, 2023) and SpaceX announcing its policy through an internal email (Mac, 2022). Finally, note that enforcement intensity of the mandates likely differed across the three companies. This is hard to know with certainty because it concerns internal company policy. However, it is immaterial to the extent that the policies constituted a credible threat when announced. Indeed, while the media reported that office attendance at Microsoft did not reach its 50% target in the first few months after their RTO (Roberts, 2024), suggesting lenient enforcement, we nonetheless estimate a significant counterfactual decrease in senior employees following the mandate.

For each of the three companies, we construct a sample of control units by retaining only those firms that 1) had no layoffs in the sample period of three quarters around the RTO; 2) either never implemented an RTO or implemented it at least one quarter after the end of the sample period; 3) fell under the three NAICS codes most commonly associated with the tech industry -- Information (51), Professional, Scientific and Technical Services (54), or Manufacturing (33) --; and 4) had at least 5% of the total number of resumes observed for the treated unit, to guarantee comparability. Together, these restrictions leave us with a sample size of 1,141,518 employment-by-quarter observations for 32 total companies in our sample for Microsoft.55
5

Note that LinkedIn, a subsidiary of Microsoft, is in the sample, but it only implemented an RTO over a year after Microsoft did (Stewart, 2023) and is fully independent. An “employment” here means a single employment of an individual at a given company, where an employee changing job can have two employments within a quarter.

sections.name: Descriptives
sections.text:
The data reveal several descriptive patterns that speak to our main results. In Table 2, we report cross-company summary statistics for our main variables of interest in the quarter before Microsoft’s RTO. Specifically, we first aggregate several variables across employees within each company in our main sample and then report the dispersion across companies. This shows that the average tenure at the companies in our sample is around 2.5 years, and the title held by the median employee at most of the companies is at either the manager (4) or senior (5) level. We observe between 2,700 and 80,000 resumes at any of the firms, giving us ample statistical power to estimate the empirical tenure distribution. Moreover, the quarterly turnover is in line with estimates for the information and professional sectors from the Bureau of Labor Statistics’s Job Openings and Turnover Survey (https://www.bls.gov/jlt/); while the share of female employees aligns with other estimates of around 30% (Bureau of Labor Statistics and NCWIT, 2021). Finally, 5% of employees that left their company within the quarter of interest took up positions at startups, which we classify as firms with fewer than 50 employees. To supplement these statistics, Appendix Table A-2 reports observable characteristics of Microsoft, the control pool, and the synthetic control. These raw comparisons are descriptive and should not be interpreted as the relevant balance condition for the synthetic control design. Under the distributional linear model described below, the identifying condition is stated in terms of pre-treatment outcome distributions: if the treated firm’s pre-treatment tenure or seniority distribution is matched by the distributional synthetic control, the same weights recover the untreated post-treatment counterfactual distribution under the model. Thus, under this model, separate balance on observed covariates is not required for identification once the relevant pre-treatment distributions are matched. This approach is analogous to assuming the linear factor model in Abadie et al. (2010) does not contain observed covariates. Covariate balance of the synthetic control can nevertheless be useful as an auxiliary diagnostic for the plausibility of the assumption of common dynamics implied by the linear model.

A preview of the main descriptive results is shown in Figure 2. There, we display the observed distributions of our main outcome variables, seniority and tenure, in the quarter before (“Pre”) and after (“Post”) Microsoft’s RTO. Looking at the tenure distribution in the top row, we can see that both the probability density function and the quantile function shift leftward after the RTO, suggesting a decrease in the total days tenured across the distribution. Similarly, in the bottom row, we observe an increase in the histogram density for employees at the trainee level and a decrease at the senior level. This corresponds to a leftward shift in the cumulative probability at seniority levels below “manager” in 2(d). Overall, the patterns in the raw data already suggest a decrease in tenure and seniority at Microsoft after its RTO. Of course, these patterns are only correlational insofar as they do not account for how the distributions would have evolved in the absence of a return to office. As such, they fail to account for confounding shocks unrelated to the RTO mandate. This is the purpose of our synthetic controls approach, which we describe and estimate in the next section.

Finally, we show the network of companies to which Microsoft employees left in Figure 3, for the quarter before and after its RTO. Each vertex indicates a company to which an employee moved. The vertex sizes correspond to the median tenure the newly hired employees had accumulated at Microsoft before leaving. Thus, the networks draw a picture of the outflow of experience from Microsoft to other large firms in related industries. That way, one can observe a marked increase in the median tenure of employees hired at several large tech companies that compete directly with Microsoft for labor, such as Meta, Snap Inc., and Intel, as well as in several other companies that are less obviously direct competitors such as Boeing. In other words, after Microsoft’s RTO, several senior employees appear to have moved to other large, tech or tech-adjacent firms that did not have an RTO mandate in place, some of which were direct competitors of Microsoft. We find causal support for these descriptive patterns by estimating a counterfactual decrease in employees’ tenure and seniority at Microsoft, as well as an increase in the share of employees departing for larger companies instead of startups.

sections.name: Estimation
sections.text:
The descriptive patterns documented above can only provide correlational evidence, as they do not account for counterfactual changes that would have affected Microsoft’s employee distribution in the absence of an RTO. In particular, one could expect companies to implement an RTO mandate because of pre-existing issues with employee retention, leading to endogeneity concerns.
In order to estimate the counterfactual distribution, we use the distributional synthetic controls estimator from Gunsilius (2023). The idea is to extend the classical synthetic controls method (Abadie and Gardeazabal, 2003; Abadie et al., 2010; Abadie, 2021) to settings where the policy change of interest is implemented at an aggregate level, but the researcher has access to disaggregated data. This is exactly our setting, where the level of intervention is at the company level, but the heterogeneity of the treatment is of fundamental interest. The distributional synthetic controls estimator is ideally suited for this setting as it estimates the heterogeneous treatment effect for the entire company and not an individual treatment effect for each unique worker. In particular, the method does not make the common assumption that individuals can be tracked over time. Relaxing this assumption allows for changes in the composition of workers due to both entry and exit into the company, which is a crucial aspect of within-firm employee distributions.

The classical synthetic controls method was developed for observational settings where treatment is not randomly assigned to units. Furthermore, the pool of control units is sufficiently dissimilar from the treated unit that simple before-and-after comparisons of outcome trends, as in the difference-in-differences design, are hard to defend. The method proposes to solve these challenges to causal inference by closely replicating the behavior of the treated unit prior to treatment. This becomes feasible when the pool of control units is sufficiently large. This is exactly the setting considered in this paper, where RTO policies are non-random, strategic decisions by firms, and employment trends at firms that do and do not return to the office are likely to differ. The argument is that, if one can construct a “synthetic Microsoft” that replicates the employment trends at Microsoft well enough in the months before its RTO, one can use it as a “synthetic control” unit afterward.

We briefly review the idea behind the distributional version of synthetic controls. For more detailed information, we refer to Gunsilius (2023) and the R implementation (Van Dijcke et al., 2024). Denote by F_{jt,N}(y) the cumulative distribution function of the outcome of interest Y —in our case seniority or tenure—for company j at time t in the absence of the intervention. The distribution in the presence of intervention is denoted by F_{jt,I} . We write t^{*} for the last time point before the policy’s implementation. By construction, the observed distribution F_{jt} coincides with F_{jt,N} for all t\leq t^{*} . We denote the corresponding quantile function by

In our setting the distributions F_{jt} are estimated from individual level data Y_{i(t)jt} , where i(t) is the individual i at company j at time t . Individual observations are only used to estimate the distributions \hat{F}_{jtn} and corresponding quantiles \hat{F}^{-1}_{jtn} , where n is the number of cross-sectional observations in time period t , which is allowed to vary with both t and j .

In the synthetic controls setting, we pick a target company j=0 that at a point t^{*}+1 implements the RTO mandate. We focus on Microsoft as our target company but replicate our main results for SpaceX and Apple. We only use companies as potential controls that had not implemented a form of RTO three months after the end of the sample period, or equivalently six months after the target company’s RTO. Our goal is to estimate the counterfactual distribution F_{0t,N} for time periods t>t^{*} to see what would have happened to the outcome distribution of the target company had it not implemented the RTO mandate.

We have two main outcomes of interest, tenure at the company in number of days and seniority in terms of an employee’s title. We treat tenure as a continuous variable. Therefore, we estimate the counterfactual tenure distribution by obtaining the optimal weights \vec{\lambda}^{*}_{t}=\left(\lambda_{1t},\ldots,\lambda_{Jt}\right) in each time period t\leq t^{*} , by solving

From the resulting time-specific weights, we form one set of time-averaged weights \vec{\lambda}^{*}=\frac{1}{t^{*}}\sum_{t=1}^{t^{*}}\vec{\lambda}_{t}^{*} , and construct the counterfactual quantile function for the time periods t>t^{*} via

Here, \Delta^{J}=\left\{(\lambda_{1t},\ldots,\lambda_{Jt})\in\mathbb{R}^{J}:\lambda_{1t},\ldots,\lambda_{Jt}\geq 0,\quad\sum_{j=1}^{J}\lambda_{j}=1\right\} is the probability unit simplex in \mathbb{R}^{J} . In this sense, the distributional version is the perfect analogue of the classic synthetic controls estimator of Abadie and Gardeazabal (2003), which also generates one set of time-invariant weights by averaging. The other outcome variable is seniority, which is a discrete variable with 10 ordinal values. Since the outcome is ordinal and not cardinal, it makes sense to use mixtures of distributions instead of mixtures of quantiles, as distributions preserve the ordinal structure. Therefore, in line with the arguments in Gunsilius (2023), we compute the optimal weights \vec{\lambda}^{*,\mathrm{title}}_{t} in this case via

and construct the counterfactual distribution in t>t^{*} via

We also use this mixture of distributions approach to estimate the counterfactual share of leavers with a certain characteristic in Section 3.2.

To obtain an unbiased causal effect of RTO on the tenure distribution using the synthetic controls, we rely on the causal model for distributional synthetic controls introduced in Gunsilius (2023, Appendix A). The model assumes that the outcome of an individual i at company j aft time t can be written as Y_{ijt,N}=\alpha_{t}+\beta_{t}U_{ijt} , for U_{ijt}=\gamma_{t}+\delta_{t}U_{ij(t-1)} , where i indexes the individual, j indexes the company and t indexes time. The latent variable U_{ijt} summarizes worker- and firm-level determinants of the potential outcome absent the RTO, such as accumulated firm-specific human capital, career stage, and latent retention propensity. The parameters \alpha_{t} and \beta_{t} allow the mapping from this latent component to the observed outcome to vary over time, while \gamma_{t} and \delta_{t} describe the common evolution and persistence of the latent component. This model relies on the linearity assumption to identify the treatment effect—analogously to the classic synthetic controls model (Abadie et al., 2010), but through a distributional reduced-form structure rather than a linear factor model. In our setting, the linearity assumption is a tractable approximation over the short estimation window of a few quarters. The latent component captures persistent characteristics such as firm-specific human capital and match quality that plausibly evolve smoothly over short horizons. Moreover, while some such structure is necessary—pre-treatment fit alone does not identify the counterfactual—exact linearity is sufficient but not the only possibility, and weaker distributional factor structures can also suffice. For a factor model approach at the quantile level for distributional synthetic controls, see also Zhang et al. (2026).

Unlike approaches based on unconfoundedness, this does not require treatment to be independent of potential outcomes given observed covariates: RTO adoption may depend on a firm’s unobserved latent type, so long as the dynamics governing it are common across units. Moreover, unlike changes-in-changes (Athey and Imbens, 2006), this approach identifies counterfactual distributions at the company level j rather than the individual level i , which means the method works with repeated cross-sections where the individuals i observed within each unit j can vary over time. Gunsilius (2023) contains a formal proof that the causal effect in this model is identified from the proposed distributional synthetic controls estimator under the condition that it replicates the pre-treatment treated unit’s distribution.

To construct confidence intervals, we rely on a version of the bootstrap. The bootstrap algorithm we
use as well as conditions that guarantee its uniform convergence, which we prove as a novel
theoretical contribution, are provided in Appendix E. It is different from existing results, since we only prove that the bootstrap works almost everywhere under the assumption that the quantile functions are sampled from some random measure that is absolutely continuous with respect to a Gaussian measure. While this assumption is unconventional in the classical asymptotic theory, it is reasonable in our setting since we work with entire quantile functions. In fact, this allows us to address ideas of randomness at the level of the quantile function, which fits our functional data framework. We report uniform confidence bands throughout to account for simultaneous inference. Monte Carlo simulations, reported in Appendix E.1, validate that the confidence bands achieve uniform nominal coverage, barring some slight undercoverage that is common for functional data (Degras, 2011; Chernozhukov et al., 2014, e.g.), for a data-generating process tailored to mimic the empirical application, and converge approximately at rate \sqrt{n} , supporting the theoretical results. For the continuous quantile-function estimator, we report uniform confidence bands to account for simultaneous inference. We also report analogous bootstrap bands for the discrete CDF-mixture analyses, while the formal validity result in Appendix E applies to the quantile-function estimator.

Finally, we perform inference via a permutation test, analogous to the classical setting (Abadie et al., 2010). The intuition is the same as in the classic case: we apply the same synthetic control method to each control unit, pretending it is the treated unit. If there is a treatment effect, the actual treated unit should be among the units with the most dramatic post-treatment change compared to these ’placebo’ tests. Since we work with distributions instead of vectors, we rely on the same distance we used to replicate the pre-treatment trends: the Wasserstein distance. To account for suboptimal fits in the replications of the pre-treatment distributions, we augment the proposed test in Gunsilius (2023) and construct a novel permutation test as the ratio of post-to-pre-intervention distances following Abadie et al. (2010); Abadie (2021) by computing the statistic

when treating company j as the target and calculating the p -value for the permutation test as

where H(x) is the Heaviside function, which takes the value 1 if x\geq 0 and 0 if x<0 . Here,

is the root mean squared prediction error in the distance d_{t} . For the continuous quantile-mixture estimator, we use the 2 -Wasserstein distance

For the discrete CDF-mixture estimator, we instead use the corresponding 1 -Wasserstein distance

which is the same distance used to construct the synthetic control in
(2).

The two inference approaches are complementary. The permutation test provides an overall test of causal significance under the sharp null hypothesis that no unit is affected by treatment; it is nonparametric and valid in finite samples under exchangeability of treatment assignment across units. The bootstrap confidence bands, by contrast, are for analyzing the purely statistical randomness induced by the fact that in practice the quantile functions have to be estimated themselves. For the continuous quantile-function estimator, their validity relies on asymptotic arguments based on Hadamard differentiability of the synthetic controls functional; see Appendix E. These arguments require the number of observations within each firm-quarter to be large.

sections.name: The causal effects of an RTO on tenure and seniority
sections.text:
Using the method described above, we estimate synthetic counterfactual tenure and title distributions for Microsoft. For the tenure distribution, we restrict the distribution to the bottom 90 quantiles as the top 10 quantiles are very sparse, leading to unstable estimates. In Table 3, we report the top 10 largest control weights for each of the two outcomes of interest separately, together with the name of the corresponding control unit. Most of the companies receiving the largest weights in both outcomes of interest are highly similar to Microsoft, being large diversified tech firms that produce both hardware and software, such as Amazon, Dell, Motorola, and Cisco. The weights differ somewhat across outcomes because different control firms may better approximate Microsoft’s tenure distribution versus its title distribution. This is not a concern for identification: each outcome has its own synthetic control constructed to match that specific outcome in the pre-period. Despite these weight differences, the qualitative conclusions are consistent across both outcomes.

With these weights in hand, we construct a distributional synthetic control for Microsoft. We find that the implementation of a return-to-office mandate in April 2022 led to a significant shift in the composition of employee departures, with more senior staff leaving at higher rates. Figure 4 depicts this through the counterfactual changes in employee tenure.

For the left panel, the y-axis captures the difference between the observed distribution of tenure in number of days and the counterfactual one, estimated using the distributional synthetic controls method. The x-axis represents quantiles of these distributions. The synthetic control can accurately reconstruct the pre-RTO tenure distribution, as the difference between the two distributions is close to and not significantly different from zero at all quantile grid points. Following the return-to-office (RTO) mandate, we estimate a reduction in tenure among Microsoft’s employees that escalates with tenure duration, and only becomes statistically significant for the top 2 deciles. With pointwise confidence bands, this becomes the top 5 deciles (not reported). In terms of magnitudes, tenure at Microsoft decreased by two months at the top deciles. Our permutation test supports the validity of this inference, with a p-value of 0.06 (0.03 for the quantiles above the median).

For an alternative perspective, we discretize the tenure measure into years and estimate the counterfactual change in the CDF of this discrete variable using the mixture of distributions approach in (2). Thus, we can interpret the y-axis as capturing the increase in probability mass at a given year of tenure. The resulting estimates are shown in the right panel of Figure 4. We replicate the pre-treatment distributions nearly perfectly. After treatment, we estimate a 2% increase in the probability mass of employees that have 0 to 3 years of tenure, corresponding to a relative decrease in the share of employees with longer tenure. Again, the permutation p-value of 0.06 supports the validity of the inference. We note that the ends of the support for all categorical variables in this paper have a 0% change in the CDF by construction, but nonetheless have confidence bands around them due to the nature of uniform confidence bands.

In Figure 5, we consider a different measure of the employee distribution: seniority. The figure depicts an increase in the mass of workers with lower-ranking titles at Microsoft after its RTO, using the mixture of distributions approach in (2). We estimate an increase in the mass of employees in training, entry, and manager positions of approximately 1.7%, with the corresponding bootstrap bands excluding zero. The estimator replicates the pre-treatment distribution well, with the bootstrap bands including zero everywhere. We obtain nearly identical results when restricting the distribution to only the senior level and below, where most of the mass is concentrated. The permutation test once again supports the validity of the inference, with a p-value of 0.03. While the CDF is the fundamental object of analysis in our categorical setting, we also report these results for changes in the corresponding PMF in Figure A-3, which may be easier to interpret. An additional benefit is that the PMF better captures the decreases in mass at the top of the title distribution, for which the bootstrap bands also exclude zero for SpaceX. Additionally, these results are nearly unchanged when pooling the Owner, Partner, and Director categories together in Figure A-4, to account for the fact that not all firms may have Owner or Partner positions.

We replicate these results almost identically for Apple and SpaceX in Figure A-2. The result for the continuous tenure distribution does not replicate, likely because we observe fewer resumes at these companies, which makes it harder to accurately estimate the continuous tenure distribution. This explanation is supported by the bad pre-treatment fit of the tenure distribution for these companies (not reported). However, when we discretize it into 5-year bins in Figure A-1, we estimate an increase in the mass of workers with less than 5 years of tenure of 1.5%. To replicate the result for the title distribution, we focus on the titles below the senior level at these companies, as there is very little mass at the higher titles.66
6

The results for Microsoft replicate identically when restricting the distribution in this way. Interestingly, the magnitude of the results appears to increase with the stringency of the RTO, with Apple seeing a leftward shift in mass of up to 2% and no significant effects for managers, while up to 5% of the SpaceX distribution shifts leftward. This correlates with these companies mandating 1 and 5 days of office attendance each week, respectively, compared to Microsoft’s 50%.

Several points merit further discussion. First, the distribution of some of our control units may be affected by spillover effects, if one of the employees leaving Microsoft takes up employment at a control unit. We do not believe this will meaningfully bias our estimates, as only 5% of employees leave a company in a given quarter, on average. Of those, we typically see only a handful of these leaving for the same, usually large, firm. Furthermore, we restricted our control sample to companies with at least 5% of the number of employees observed at Microsoft, so the number of employees joining any single control unit will be trivial relative to that unit’s total number of employees. Together, these facts imply that any bias due to potential spillover effects to control units is likely negligible. To verify this claim, we track where Microsoft employees go after leaving the company post-RTO. Of all Microsoft leavers in the post-treatment quarter, only 78 employees (0.16% of Microsoft’s workforce) joined any of our 31 control firms. The maximum share of any control firm’s workforce that came from Microsoft was 0.30% (Docusign), and no control firm received more than 1% of its workforce from Microsoft (Table A-3). Moreover, any such spillovers would bias our estimates toward zero: if senior Microsoft employees join control firms, this mechanically increases the average tenure at those firms, making the synthetic control’s tenure distribution shift rightward and reducing the estimated treatment effect. As a bounding exercise, we re-estimate our main specification excluding the five control firms that received the most Microsoft employees post-RTO. The permutation test p -value remains stable with Microsoft ranked 2nd, confirming that our results are robust to potential spillover effects (Table A-4).

Second, there could be anticipation effects that bias the magnitude of our estimates. For all three companies we consider, however, the RTO mandates were announced less than 2 months prior to their implementation.77
7

Microsoft announced plans for a phased return to the office in early February 2022 with mandatory office presence from April 2022 onwards (Tilley and Cutter, 2022). Apple announced its RTO mandate, which took effect in April 2022, in early March (Haring, 2022); while SpaceX’s RTO was announced with immediate effect via an internal email from Elon Musk to employees (Mac, 2022). Given that a typical job search takes around 4.5 months on average (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024) and resignations usually only take effect at the end of the month, this left essentially no room for anticipation that is not captured by our research design. Of course, employees may have heard rumors before the official announcement. Both Microsoft and Apple, however, delayed several prior RTOs indefinitely due to pushback from employees and pandemic conditions (O’Loughlin, 2023; O’Loughlin, 2022). Survey evidence from May 2022 indeed suggested that such pushback to office attendance requirements had been common and effective (Bloom, 2022). Thus, it seems likely that employees only acted on the mandates once they were actually implemented due to the uncertainty surrounding them as well as their previous successes in pushing back the dates. This does not contradict the possibility that employees planning to leave had already started their job search before the actual RTO, which would explain the sizeable tenure effects we observe only 3 months after implementation.

Third, due to the interference of layoff dates with RTO mandates, we are only able to study these mandates’ effects one quarter after their implementation. It is possible that firms try to mitigate the documented shift in their tenure distribution after their RTO by increased hiring or internal promotions. This does not negate the significant costs associated with this shift and any mitigation thereof, which we discuss in more detail below.

Fourth, an important question is whether the compositional shift we document is driven by senior employees departing or by differential hiring of junior employees. To address this, we apply standard synthetic control methods (Abadie et al., 2010) to aggregate separation and hiring rates. We focus on Microsoft for this exercise, since it has a much larger sample size, providing more power for accurately estimating effects on the much smaller sets of leavers and joiners and their subsequent destinations. Table 4 reports the results. Neither Microsoft’s separation rate ( p=0.219 ) nor its hiring rate ( p=1 ) differs significantly from the synthetic control. The precision of this null is limited: the placebo distributions of post-RTO flow-rate effects are wide (10th–90th percentile range [-1.3,+0.6] pp for separations and [-1.5,+0.8] pp for hiring; s.d. \approx 1 pp), so Table 4 can rule out flow-rate effects larger than roughly \pm 1.5 percentage points but cannot exclude smaller changes. Net employee flows were positive across all seniority levels post-RTO but this reflects the broader tech hiring boom in early 2022 rather than anything specific to Microsoft, as control firms exhibited nearly identical patterns. Importantly, the June spike in entry-level hiring associated with new college graduates is accounted for by the synthetic control; the DiSCo-weighted counterfactual exhibits a similarly large June spike as Microsoft (46.4% vs. 62.6% entry-level share among new hires). The aggregate null should therefore be read as “no large change in volumes” while the mechanism is identified through the composition of leavers (Section B.2) rather than aggregate rates.

Appendix B studies this mechanism in greater detail. Using synthetic control methods on the characteristics of separating employees, we find that the mean tenure of leavers at Microsoft increased by 110.8 days relative to the counterfactual ( p=0.032 ), and the share of leavers with senior titles rose by 8.4 percentage points ( p=0.097 ). The composition of new hires, by contrast, was unchanged, with the same caveat about precision as above. The RTO thus changed who left, not how many left, with junior employees staying at higher rates and offsetting the increase in senior departures. This pattern is consistent with Emanuel et al. (2023), who find that the productivity gains from office proximity are concentrated among junior employees still building firm-specific human capital, who as a result may be more inclined to stay after an RTO mandate.

Finally, the results are robust to extending the pre-treatment period out further to three quarters before the RTO mandates, as shown in Appendix A.3.

sections.name: Where Do Employees Go After an RTO?
sections.text:
Our main results provide robust evidence that long-tenured and senior employees depart from Microsoft at higher rates after it implements a return to office mandate. A natural follow-up question to ask is: where do these senior employees go? To answer this question, we construct a set of distributional synthetic controls for the employees who leave Microsoft in a given quarter. Since the leavers comprise a far smaller sample than the total number of employees, we focus on replicating an aggregate distributional statistic (Abadie et al., 2010), the share of leavers who have characteristic X, rather than the entire distribution.

This way, we find that Microsoft’s RTO led to a counterfactual decrease in the share of its employees departing for startups, as shown in Figure 6. In particular, we proxy for whether a firm is a start-up in two ways: whether it has fewer than 50 employees, and whether it is below the 5th quantile in terms of its industry labor share. For both measures, we estimate an increase in the mass of workers leaving to non-startups of around 5% that is significant at the 95% level. Moreover, the permutation test for both measures indicates the inference is (marginally) valid, with p-values of 0.03 and 0.09, respectively. Combined with our main finding that more senior employees are leaving at higher rates, this result aligns with the descriptive evidence in Figure 3 that the RTO caused a departure of senior employees to other large firms. Thus, Microsoft’s RTO appears to not only have had important human capital costs due to the hiring and training costs required to replace the senior employees lost, but also potential competitive side effects due to these employees taking operational knowledge with them.

Finally, in Figure A-5 we further test for, but fail to find any evidence of, distributional differences in: the share of men vs. women leaving Microsoft; the share of leavers that go into unemployment; the share of leavers that accept a demotion in their title at their new job; and the share of leavers changing roles at their new job. The lack of gender differences is notable given prior survey and experimental evidence that women report stronger preferences for working from home (YouGov, 2022; Pelta, 2021; Mas and Pallais, 2017); in our setting, however, we do not find evidence that the RTO induced differential exits by gender. The lack of counterfactual changes in unemployment status, demotions, and job roles suggests that the senior employees leaving Microsoft have good outside options, in the sense that they appear to find employment in similar roles and levels of seniority. Of course, given employees’ well-documented willingness to pay for remote work (Mas and Pallais, 2017), they may have accepted wage cuts. Unfortunately, the PDL data does not contain accurate salary information, so we cannot test for this. Nonetheless, our other findings align with the fact that Microsoft implemented its RTO mandate much earlier than most tech companies, which meant there were still many fully remote companies the leavers could go to. As such, we can expect the value of employees’ outside option to shrink as more companies implement RTOs.

At the same time, this also suggests that the share of companies in an industry that have returned to office will determine the negative impact of an RTO mandate on the company that implements it. That is because, all else equal, we can expect that the outflow of senior employees that we have documented will be larger when these employees’ outside options are better. This hints at the existence of a tipping point where companies implement RTO mandates at increasing rates when the value of employees’ outside options has diminished sufficiently. As a counterpoint, many companies started explicitly coding the degree of hybrid work allowed into new joiners’ contracts, which may generate path dependence both for fully remote companies as well as those that returned to the office. We provide suggestive evidence that a more slack labor market attenuates the compositional effects we document in Appendix D, where we replicate our analysis for Amazon and Google. Both firms implemented their RTO mandate in 2023, in the midst of a sector-wide wave of layoffs, which significantly weakened the tech sector’s labor market. Indeed, both firms conducted large-scale layoffs themselves in the months leading up to their RTO. As such, the RTO policy intervention is almost certainly confounded by these layoffs, and these results should be interpreted with caution. We focus on these two firms as they have by far the largest sample sizes among the set of firms that implemented RTOs early on in this tech layoff wave. Nonetheless, we find some evidence that the effects we document are indeed fully attenuated at these firms. At the same time, another study by Ding et al. (2024) has replicated our key results of a “brain drain” for 54 S&P 500 firms with RTO mandates between Q1 2020 and Q4 2023 using a difference-in-differences design, providing independent evidence for the external validity of our findings.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text:
This article estimates that a return-to-office mandate at Microsoft led to a significant outflow of senior employees to large firms, some of which are direct Microsoft competitors. What does this suggest about the larger ramifications of such mandates for the companies that implement them?
To start, consider the reasons for implementing an RTO mandate. Managers tend to believe work-from-home decreases productivity (Bloom, Barrero, Davis, Meyer and Mihaylov, 2023b) and diffusion of knowledge within the firm (Barrero et al., 2023), and face difficulties monitoring employees in remote-work settings (Microsoft, 2022). The academic literature provides support for some, but not all, of these concerns – see Barrero et al. (2023) for an overview. On the other hand, employee satisfaction and retention have been found to be lower in in-person work settings (Bloom et al., 2015; Choudhury et al., 2024). Our results suggest that such retention issues may be more serious than previously thought, as senior employees and, indeed, the (senior) managers themselves are leaving. Moreover, the sudden shift induced by an RTO mandate may cause a large, temporary spike in employee attrition, which can have quantitatively and qualitatively different effects from chronic but gradual attrition. Thus, a firm returning to the office with the aim of increasing productivity or innovation may end up doing so in a narrow sense, improving the output metrics of those who stay, but harming those metrics for the company as a whole.

In support of this, the academic literature provides ample evidence on the value of senior and long-tenured employees to the companies they work at. In broad terms, human capital has been theorized to be a key factor determining firms’ competitive advantage and estimated to be strongly related to firm performance (Crook et al., 2011). More specifically, worker output has been found to be monotonically increasing in tenure (Shaw and Lazear, 2008), with bosses estimated to be almost two times as productive as the average worker (Lazear et al., 2015). These effects are driven by (costly) employee training (De Grip and Sauermann, 2012; Konings and Vanormelingen, 2015) and the more general accrual of firm-specific human capital with tenure (Becker, 1962). Moreover, senior employees tend to not just be productive; they also strongly affect a firm’s wider productivity. Managers and management practices have been found to explain a large share of the variation in firm productivity (Bender et al., 2018; Metcalfe et al., 2023; Fenizia, 2022), especially in combination with higher-quality human capital (Bender et al., 2018). Employees working in research and development (R&D) not only increase a firm’s innovation rates, but also take their accumulated knowledge with them when they move to competitors (Palomeras and Melero, 2010; Cassiman and Veugelers, 2006). Relatedly, lower employee turnover has been found to increase firm investment and decrease new firm entry (Jeffers, 2024). Replacing skilled employees also incurs substantial hiring costs, equal to around 2–4 months of pay, that increase with the skill level (Blatter et al., 2012).

As discussed above, RTO mandates are implemented strategically by firms. Hence, it is natural to ask to what extent the employment consequences we document in this paper were intended. While it is possible that this was partially the case, it seems unlikely that this fully explains the effects we document, for two reasons. One, their magnitude. In the absence of large-scale layoffs, which we manually ascertained did not happen for any of the firms in our sample, it seems unlikely that firms intended their RTO mandate to cause 5% of senior employees to leave. We validate this by re-estimating our main results for the January 2023 layoffs at Microsoft in Appendix C. That way, we do not find significant effects of the layoff on either the tenure or title distribution, supporting our argument that the observed results are not driven by concurrent layoffs, which appear to not affect the workforce composition. Two, firms’ forecasting abilities. Given the unpredictable nature of employee response, and limited forecasting technology, it seems unlikely that firms were able to predict precisely how their employees would respond to an RTO mandate. This hypothesis appears to be supported by the many articles documenting employee resistance to announced mandates, and subsequent backtracking on the firm side. It thus seems reasonable to consider the employment effects documented here as mostly unintentional side effects of RTO mandates.

Taken together, this large body of literature implies that increased attrition of senior employees can substantially impede firm output, productivity, innovation, and competitiveness. This provides an important perspective on the implications of the return to office for the broader functioning of a company. Moreover, the downstream outcomes of the “uneven attrition” we document may be a fruitful avenue for future research.

sections.name: Conclusion
sections.text:
The workplace revolution brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic continues to reverberate across offices globally, even as the pandemic itself retreats into history. While some companies have returned to the office, many others have gone fully remote. This paper has provided novel evidence on the implications of this bifurcation for the distribution of employees across and within companies. In particular, we provide causal evidence that three of the largest U.S. tech companies—Microsoft, SpaceX, and Apple—experienced similar shifts toward a less senior workforce after implementing an RTO mandate, with the strongest statistical evidence for Microsoft and SpaceX.
We do this using a distributional extension of the classical synthetic controls estimator (Abadie and Gardeazabal, 2003; Gunsilius, 2023), for which we derive conditions for the uniform validity of the bootstrap. Moreover, we provide both descriptive and causal evidence that these senior employees left for larger companies at higher rates than usual. Taken together, our findings imply that return-to-office mandates can lead to significant human capital costs in terms of output, productivity, innovation, and competitiveness for the companies that implement them. Furthermore, the sorting of skilled labor across companies that our findings imply can have important consequences for the employment landscape, which we leave to future work.

sections.name: A.3 Extended Pre-Treatment Period
sections.text:
A potential concern with synthetic control methods is whether the pre-treatment period is sufficiently long to credibly establish that the synthetic control captures the treated unit’s counterfactual trajectory. Our main analysis uses two pre-treatment quarters (Q4 2021 and Q1 2022). Here we extend the analysis to include three pre-treatment quarters: Q3 2021, Q4 2021, and Q1 2022.

The extended pre-treatment period serves two purposes: (1) it provides stronger evidence that our synthetic control accurately captures Microsoft’s counterfactual trajectory, and (2) it allows us to rule out pre-existing trends in the tenure distribution that might confound our estimates.

Figure A-6 presents the results. The synthetic control continues to replicate Microsoft’s distributions nearly perfectly across all three pre-treatment quarters, with confidence intervals including zero at all quantile grid points. The post-treatment effect remains statistically significant and similar in magnitude to our original estimates.

We emphasize that the linear distributional model of Gunsilius (2023, Appendix A) is more restrictive than the linear factor model of Abadie et al. (2010), as it does not allow for multiple unobserved factor components but rather assumes strict linearity in a one-dimensional unobservable. As such, under this model, our estimator can achieve identification without requiring the pre-treatment duration to approach infinity. The extended pre-treatment period test still helps in assessing the realism of our single-dimensional factor assumption. For a multivariate distributional factor model, we again refer to Zhang et al. (2026).

sections.name: A.4 Spillover Robustness
sections.text:
A potential concern with the synthetic control approach is that control firms may experience “indirect treatment” if Microsoft employees who leave after the RTO join control firms, mechanically affecting their tenure distributions. This section quantifies the magnitude of such spillovers and demonstrates that our results are robust to their exclusion.

Table A-3 reports the destinations of Microsoft employees who left after the RTO and joined one of our 31 control firms. The spillover magnitude is negligible: only 78 Microsoft employees (0.16% of Microsoft’s workforce) joined any control firm in the post-treatment quarter. The maximum share of any control firm’s post-RTO workforce that came from Microsoft was 0.30% (Docusign), and no control firm received more than 1% of its workforce from Microsoft.

Importantly, the direction of any spillover bias is toward zero (i.e., conservative). If senior Microsoft employees join control firms, this mechanically increases the average tenure at those firms, shifting the synthetic control’s tenure distribution rightward. This would reduce the estimated gap between Microsoft and its synthetic control, making our treatment effect estimates conservative.

Table A-4 presents a bounding exercise where we re-estimate our main specification after excluding the five control firms that received the most Microsoft employees post-RTO. The permutation test p-value remains stable with Microsoft ranked second ( 2/32\approx 0.06,2/27\approx 0.07 ), confirming that spillovers do not drive our results.

sections.name: B.1 Aggregate Separation and Hiring Rates
sections.text:
Table A-5 provides descriptive context on the composition of worker flows before and after Microsoft’s RTO mandate. Several patterns emerge. In Panel A, we show the tenure composition of leavers, i.e., what seniority employees who left their companies in the given time period were. At Microsoft, the share of leavers with 5+ years tenure increased from 15.2% to 15.9% post-RTO, while the share with 0–1 years decreased from 29.9% to 22.4%. This shift towards fewer junior leavers and more senior leavers is consistent with our main finding that separations tilted toward more experienced employees. In contrast, control firms’ tenure composition remained stable (35.0% \to 35.1% for 0–1 years; 10.2% \to 9.2% for 5+ years).
Notably, Microsoft’s separators are more senior on average than controls’ even pre-RTO (15.2% vs. 10.2% with 5+ years), reflecting differences in workforce composition. In Panel B, we report the net flows by title. Both Microsoft and control firms experienced strong positive net flows post-RTO, reflecting the broader tech hiring boom in early 2022. Entry-level net flows swung from negative to sharply positive at both Microsoft and controls, capturing the June new graduate hiring spike.

While informative, these numbers do not tell us much about the counterfactual behavior of Microsoft’s workforce in the absence of their mandate, and it is clear that the numbers are heavily influenced by seasonal patterns such as entry-level hiring of new graduates (see below).
To get a better sense of the causal effects of the mandate on Microsoft’s aggregate hiring and firing flows, we apply the standard Abadie et al. (2010) synthetic control methodology separately to separation rates and hiring
rates (inflows and outflows as a percent of total workforce). We also report p-values for the classical permutation test for synthetic controls. Table
4 reports the results, which indicate that the total amount of hiring and firing taking place after Microsoft’s RTO was not significantly different from its synthetic control, though we see a spike in hiring for both Microsoft and the control firms in the post-treatment period, driven by hiring of new graduates (see Section B.3).

Indeed, as we show in Section B.2 below, the RTO effect operates through the composition of
separations (i.e., who leaves) rather than through differential aggregate rates. This distinction is
important: even with similar overall separation rates, the mix of leavers shifted toward more senior
employees at Microsoft. The RTO effect operates not through differential volumes of hiring or
separation, but through the composition of who leaves, as documented in Table A-6.
Figure A-7 shows the synthetic control estimates for separation and hiring rates over
time. The left panel shows Microsoft’s separation rate relative to its synthetic control; the right panel
shows the same for hiring rates. The synthetic control achieves excellent pre-treatment fit for both
outcomes.

sections.name: B.2 Composition of New Hires and Departures
sections.text:
To directly test whether senior employees left at elevated rates, we analyze the composition of new and separating employees—that is, the characteristics of those who joined and left, conditional on joining or leaving.

Table A-6 reports synthetic control estimates for the share of separating employees with high tenure or senior titles.

The key finding is that the mean tenure of Microsoft employees who left increased by 110.8 days relative to the synthetic control ( p=0.032 ). The share of separating employees with senior titles (level 5+) increased by 8.4 percentage points ( p=0.097 ). These results provide direct evidence that the RTO mandate shifted the composition of departures toward more senior, higher-tenure employees.

If Microsoft were simultaneously pursuing a junior hiring strategy, we would expect to see changes in the composition of new hires. Table A-7 reports synthetic control estimates for the share of new hires with senior titles.

We find no significant changes in the composition of new hires for any specification. The share of senior employees among new hires did not change significantly ( -4.1 pp, p=0.903 ), nor did mean title level ( -0.36 , p=0.871 ). This null result rules out the alternative explanation that compositional shifts in the workforce were driven by differential hiring of junior employees rather than departures of senior employees.

sections.name: B.3 Seasonal Hiring Patterns: June New Graduate Spike
sections.text:
A potential concern is whether our main distributional synthetic control adequately captures seasonal hiring patterns, particularly the June spike in entry-level hiring associated with new college graduates. To address this, we use the same DiSCo weights from our main tenure distribution analysis to construct a synthetic control for hiring patterns.

Table A-8 shows the validation results. We compare entry-level hiring shares for Microsoft versus the DiSCo-weighted synthetic controls.

We find that the DiSCo-weighted synthetic control exhibits a similarly large June spike as Microsoft. Microsoft’s entry-level share jumps from 3.1% in non-June months to 62.6% in June (a 59.5 pp spike), while the DiSCo-weighted SC jumps from 2.7% to 46.4% (a 43.7 pp spike). Moreover, the difference in the precise magnitudes is not statistically significant: a permutation test that builds an analogous synthetic control for each control firm and treats its June entry-level prediction error as a placebo yields a p -value of 0.22 for Microsoft, so the seasonal spike is reproduced within sampling error.

This directly addresses the concern about differential junior hiring: the June new graduate hiring pattern is accounted for by the synthetic control counterfactual, and so does not drive our results.

Figure A-8 visualizes this pattern, showing that Microsoft’s entry-level hiring spike in June is matched by its DiSCo-weighted synthetic control.

sections.name: B.4 Discussion
sections.text:
The analyses in this appendix and Table 4 establish several key facts:

1.

Aggregate rates show null effects: Neither Microsoft’s separation rate ( p=0.219 ) nor its hiring rate ( p=1 ) differs significantly from controls. The RTO did not cause a detectable change in how many employees left or were hired in aggregate.

2.

Composition of leavers shifted toward seniors: The mean tenure of Microsoft employees who separated increased by 110.8 days relative to the synthetic control ( p=0.032 ), and the share with senior titles increased by 8.4 pp ( p=0.097 ).

3.

No change in new hire composition: The share of senior employees among new hires did not change significantly, providing no evidence of a concurrent junior hiring strategy. Together with the previous bullet, this suggests that senior employees left at higher rates, but this was offset by a decreased departure rate among junior employees, explaining the null effects on the overall hiring and separation rates. This finding is in line with recent literature which found that the gains from office proximity are concentrated among less-tenured and younger employees who are building human capital (Emanuel et al., 2023), providing a potential explanation for the differential departures we estimate after a return to office.

4.

Seasonal patterns accounted for: The DiSCo-weighted synthetic control exhibits a large June new graduate spike, close to that of Microsoft (46.4% vs. 62.6%), demonstrating that seasonal hiring patterns do not drive our distributional effects.

Together, these results support our interpretation that RTO mandates changed who left but not how many left. The composition of departures shifted toward more senior, higher-tenure employees, while aggregate separation and hiring rates remained similar to control firms.

sections.name: D.1 Labor Market Context
sections.text:
Table A-10 documents the dramatic shift in labor market conditions between our 2022 RTOs and the 2023 RTOs.

The 2023 labor market was characterized by substantially higher unemployment, fewer job openings, lower quit rates, and a wave of tech layoffs that had begun in late 2022. Crucially, by mid-2023, a large share of tech firms had already implemented some form of RTO (approximately 35% of the tech firms in the Russell 3000 had any type of RTO policy in 2023 according to the data used in Table A-10), reducing the availability of remote-friendly alternatives for dissatisfied employees.

In particular, both Amazon and Google conducted massive layoffs in close temporal proximity to their RTO mandates (and so did all other major tech firms in our sample), as shown in Table A-11.

These layoffs likely shifted the tenure and title distributions independently of any RTO effect, making it impossible to cleanly identify the causal impact of the RTO mandate alone. Nonetheless, to get a sense of the external validity of our findings, we replicate our synthetic controls analysis for these two firms. As in the main results, we exclude control firms that have a layoff in the sample window or already had an RTO active.

sections.name: D.2 Results
sections.text:
Table A-12 reports the permutation test p-values alongside our 2022 results.

Strikingly, we find no significant distributional effects for either Amazon or Google in 2023. The tenure p-values are 1.00 (Amazon) and 0.48 (Google); title p-values are 0.75 and 0.24, respectively, far from being statistically significant. Figure A-10 shows the estimated quantile treatment effects with confidence bands.

sections.name: D.3 Interpretation
sections.text:
We interpret the null results for 2023 cautiously, as they admit two distinct explanations.

1.

Layoff confounding: The massive layoffs at Amazon and Google in early 2023 likely already shifted the workforce composition before the RTO took effect. If layoffs disproportionately affected certain tenure or seniority groups, this would contaminate any RTO effect.

2.

Labor market channel: In the more slack 2023 labor market, employees had fewer outside options. With higher unemployment, fewer job openings, and more firms requiring office attendance, dissatisfied senior employees may have been unable to leave for remote-friendly alternatives.

The labor-market interpretation is consistent with the 2022 effects being larger in settings with stronger outside options, although the confounding from contemporaneous layoffs prevents a formal comparison of effect magnitudes across the two periods.
The 2022 RTOs occurred in a high-outside-option environment: labor markets were tight, remote jobs were relatively abundant, and many major technology firms had not yet returned to the office. The significant effects we estimate should therefore be interpreted as the realized compositional response to an RTO when employees could actually leave their firms. As that margin becomes constrained—through layoffs, labor-market slack, or industry-wide RTO adoption—the magnitude of the response is likely to diminish.
While Amazon’s pre-treatment tenure distributions in Figure A-10 are not well-replicated, likely because of the layoffs, Google’s are. In line with the expectation that a lack of outside options attenuates our paper’s main effects, the treatment effects post-RTO are not significantly different from zero across the distribution.

sections.name: D.4 RTO Stringency Gradient
sections.text:
Additional support for this interpretation comes from examining the relationship between RTO stringency and effect magnitude across our 2022 firms:

The effect magnitude increases with the stringency of the RTO mandate. This pattern suggests that distributional effects scale with the “cost” imposed on employees, consistent with a model where employees trade off commuting costs against the value of their current position.
